name: Chin Tuck
description: A gentle isometric exercise that retrains posture by drawing the head back over the shoulders, easing strain from forward-head posture (common with desk and phone use).
steps: Sit or stand tall, looking straight ahead.
Without tilting your head up or down, gently draw your chin straight back, making a 'double chin'.
Hold for 5 seconds, feeling a stretch at the base of the skull.
Release and repeat 10 times.
targets: Suboccipital and deep neck flexor muscles
cautions: Stop if you feel dizziness or sharp pain rather than a mild stretch.

name: Neck Side Stretch
description: A classic side-of-neck stretch that relieves tightness from sleeping wrong or one-sided phone/bag carrying habits.
steps: Sit tall, drop your right ear toward your right shoulder until you feel a stretch on the left side of your neck.
Optionally rest your right hand lightly on your head for a little extra pull - no forcing.
Hold 20-30 seconds, breathing normally.
Switch sides.
cautions: Avoid pulling hard on the head; the stretch should feel mild, never sharp.

name: Seated Neck Rotation
description: Restores rotational range of motion in the neck, useful for stiffness that makes checking blind spots or looking over your shoulder uncomfortable.
steps: Sit tall and slowly turn your head to look over one shoulder as far as comfortable.
Hold 10-15 seconds.
Return to center and repeat on the other side.
Do 5 slow rotations each direction.
cautions: Keep the motion slow and controlled; avoid quick jerking rotations.

name: Isometric Neck Press
description: Builds neck stability by resisting gentle self-applied pressure in each direction, often recommended alongside stretches for chronic neck tension.
steps: Place your palm against your forehead and press your head into your hand without letting your head move.
Hold 5 seconds, breathing normally.
Repeat pressing against the back, then each side of your head.
Do 5 reps in each direction.
cautions: Use gentle, steady pressure - this is about stability, not a strength max.

name: Relaxed Jaw Opening
description: A gentle mobility drill for jaw tightness or clenching-related discomfort (TMJ-area tension), encouraging a symmetric, relaxed opening pattern.
steps: Rest your tongue gently on the roof of your mouth just behind your front teeth.
Let your jaw drop open slowly and evenly, without shifting to one side.
Open until you feel mild tension, not pain, then close slowly.
Repeat 10 times, moving slowly throughout.
cautions: If you have diagnosed TMJ disorder, clicking, or locking, check with a dentist or physical therapist before doing jaw exercises.

name: Masseter Self-Massage
description: Manual release for the jaw muscles that tighten from clenching, grinding, or stress.
steps: Place two fingers on the muscle bulge at the back of your jaw (it flexes when you clench your teeth).
Apply gentle circular pressure for 30-60 seconds.
Move slightly forward along the jawline and repeat.
Do the same on the other side.
cautions: Use light pressure; this is a relaxation technique, not deep tissue work.

name: Doorway Chest Stretch
description: One of the most reliable stretches for rounded-shoulder posture, opening up tight chest muscles that pull the shoulders forward.
steps: Stand in a doorway with your forearm against the frame, elbow bent at 90 degrees, upper arm roughly shoulder height.
Step forward through the doorway slowly until you feel a stretch across the chest and front of the shoulder.
Hold 20-30 seconds.
Repeat with your arm slightly higher and slightly lower on the frame, then switch arms.
cautions: Step forward gradually; avoid a bouncing stretch or forcing shoulder pain.

name: Cross-Body Shoulder Stretch
description: Targets the back of the shoulder, useful for tightness from overhead activity or sleeping on one side.
steps: Bring your right arm straight across your chest.
Use your left forearm to gently pull the right arm closer to your chest.
Hold 20-30 seconds, keeping the shoulder relaxed away from your ear.
Switch sides.
cautions: Pull gently - this joint is mobile and easy to overstretch.

name: Pendulum Swing
description: A gentle, gravity-assisted mobility drill often used after shoulder stiffness or minor strain to restore easy motion without active muscle effort.
steps: Lean forward slightly, supporting yourself with your uninjured hand on a table or chair.
Let the affected arm hang loosely toward the floor.
Gently swing the arm in small circles, then front-to-back, letting momentum (not muscle effort) do the work.
Continue for 30-60 seconds.
cautions: Keep the arm relaxed; this should never be forced or painful.

name: Wall Slide
description: Builds overhead shoulder mobility and shoulder-blade control, helpful for people who feel 'stuck' or pinchy raising their arms overhead.
steps: Stand with your back, head, and arms against a wall, elbows bent at 90 degrees like a goalpost.
Keeping arms and lower back in contact with the wall, slide your arms upward as far as comfortable.
Slide back down with control.
Repeat 10-12 times.
targets: Rotator cuff, lower trapezius, serratus anterior
cautions: If your lower back arches off the wall or you feel pinching, reduce the range.

name: Band External Rotation
description: Strengthens the rotator cuff muscles that stabilize the shoulder, often recommended for general shoulder resilience and mild instability-related discomfort.
steps: Hold a light resistance band with elbows bent 90 degrees and tucked at your sides.
Keeping elbows pinned to your sides, rotate your forearms outward against the band.
Slowly return to start.
Do 2-3 sets of 12-15.
cautions: Use light resistance; sharp or catching pain means stop and reassess.

name: Scapular Squeeze
description: Strengthens the muscles between the shoulder blades, a common weak point behind rounded-shoulder posture and upper-back achiness.
steps: Sit or stand tall, arms relaxed at your sides.
Squeeze your shoulder blades together and slightly down, as if pinching a pencil between them.
Hold 5 seconds, then release.
Repeat 12-15 times.
cautions: Keep shoulders down, away from your ears, throughout.

name: Overhead Triceps Stretch
description: A simple stretch for the back of the upper arm, useful for tightness after overhead activity or extended time in front of a keyboard.
steps: Raise one arm overhead, then bend the elbow so your hand drops behind your head.
Use your other hand to gently press down on the bent elbow.
Hold 20-30 seconds, feeling a stretch along the back of the upper arm.
Switch sides.
cautions: Press gently on the elbow - avoid forcing extra range.

name: Doorway Biceps Stretch
description: Opens up the front of the upper arm and shoulder, a good companion to the doorway chest stretch for people who do a lot of gripping or carrying.
steps: Stand next to a doorway or wall, arm extended behind you at shoulder height, palm flat against the frame.
Slowly rotate your body away from the arm until you feel a stretch along the front of the upper arm.
Hold 20-30 seconds.
Switch sides.
cautions: Rotate slowly and stop well short of shoulder pain.

name: Foam Rolling the Upper Arm
description: A self-massage technique for general biceps/triceps tightness, often used after upper-body activity.
steps: Place a foam roller on the floor and support your upper arm on it, lying on your side or propped on your forearm.
Roll slowly from shoulder to elbow along the front or back of the arm.
Pause on tender spots for 20-30 seconds.
Repeat on the other arm.
cautions: Avoid rolling directly over the elbow joint; use light-to-moderate pressure.

name: Cat-Cow
description: A foundational spinal mobility flow that gently moves the whole spine through flexion and extension - a great general warm-up for back stiffness.
steps: Start on hands and knees, wrists under shoulders, knees under hips.
Inhale, drop your belly, lift your chest and tailbone (cow).
Exhale, round your spine toward the ceiling, tucking chin and tailbone (cat).
Flow slowly between the two for 8-10 breaths.
cautions: Move within a pain-free range; avoid forcing the end ranges.

name: Seated Thoracic Rotation
description: Restores rotation in the mid-back, which often stiffens from long sitting and can make twisting movements (like checking your back seat) feel restricted.
steps: Sit tall in a chair, arms crossed over your chest.
Keeping your hips facing forward, rotate your upper body to one side as far as comfortable.
Hold 2-3 seconds, return to center.
Repeat 10 times per side.
cautions: Keep the motion coming from the mid-back, not by twisting through the low back.

name: Thread the Needle
description: A deeper rotational stretch for the upper back and shoulder blade region, popular for relieving between-the-shoulder-blade tightness.
steps: Start on hands and knees.
Slide your right arm underneath your left arm, palm up, lowering your right shoulder and ear to the mat.
Hold 20-30 seconds, breathing into the stretch across your upper back.
Return and switch sides.
cautions: Move into the stretch slowly; avoid resting your full weight suddenly on the shoulder.

name: Foam Roller Thoracic Extension
description: Uses a foam roller to gently extend a rounded upper back, countering hours of hunched sitting.
steps: Place a foam roller horizontally under your shoulder blades, knees bent, feet flat.
Support your head with your hands, and gently arch backward over the roller.
Hold 15-20 seconds at a comfortable stretch, then curl back up.
Roll slightly up or down and repeat 5-8 times.
cautions: Support your head throughout to avoid straining your neck; avoid this if you have osteoporosis or a spinal condition without medical clearance.

name: Child's Pose
description: A gentle, restful stretch for the low back and hips - often the first thing people reach for when the low back feels tight or achy.
steps: Kneel on the floor, big toes touching, knees wide.
Sit your hips back toward your heels and walk your hands forward, lowering your chest toward the floor.
Rest your forehead down and breathe deeply.
Hold 30-60 seconds.
cautions: If it aggravates knee pain, place a cushion behind your knees or shorten the range.

name: Knee-to-Chest Stretch
description: A gentle low-back decompression stretch commonly used for general stiffness or a dull ache after prolonged sitting.
steps: Lie on your back with knees bent, feet flat.
Pull one knee toward your chest with both hands, keeping the other foot flat on the floor.
Hold 20-30 seconds, feeling a stretch through the low back and glute.
Switch legs, then try both knees together.
cautions: Avoid this if it increases leg pain, numbness, or tingling - that combination warrants a medical evaluation.

name: Pelvic Tilt
description: A gentle core-activation drill that mobilizes the low back and builds the pelvic control that underlies most low-back rehab programs.
steps: Lie on your back, knees bent, feet flat.
Flatten your low back into the floor by gently tilting your pelvis and tightening your lower abs.
Hold 5 seconds, then release to a neutral arch.
Repeat 10-15 times.
cautions: Movement should be small and controlled - this is not a big crunch.

name: Bird Dog
description: A widely used stability exercise that builds control through the low back and hips without loading the spine - a staple in most low-back care programs.
steps: Start on hands and knees, spine neutral.
Extend your right arm forward and left leg back simultaneously, keeping your hips level.
Hold 3-5 seconds without letting your low back sag or twist.
Return and switch sides, for 8-10 reps per side.
cautions: Prioritize keeping the hips and shoulders level over reaching farther.

name: Seated Forward Fold
description: A combined low-back and hamstring stretch, useful when tight hamstrings are contributing to low-back tension.
steps: Sit with legs extended in front of you, spine tall.
Hinge forward from the hips, reaching toward your feet, keeping your back long rather than rounding.
Hold at your first point of tension, 20-30 seconds.
Breathe and relax deeper into the stretch as tension eases.
cautions: Bend your knees slightly if hamstrings are very tight; never bounce.

name: Dead Bug
description: Builds core control that supports the spine during everyday movement, often prescribed alongside low-back stretches rather than as a stretch itself.
steps: Lie on your back, arms reaching toward the ceiling, knees bent 90 degrees over your hips.
Slowly lower one arm and the opposite leg toward the floor while keeping your low back flat against the mat.
Return to start and switch sides.
Do 8-10 reps per side.
cautions: Stop the range where your low back would start to arch off the floor.

name: Front Plank
description: A staple core-stability hold that builds the trunk endurance most low-back and posture programs rely on.
steps: Rest on your forearms and toes, elbows under shoulders, body in a straight line from head to heels.
Brace your abs and squeeze your glutes to keep your hips from sagging or piking up.
Hold 15-30 seconds, breathing steadily.
Rest and repeat 2-3 times.
cautions: Stop if your low back sags - shorten the hold time rather than let form break down.

name: Side Plank
description: Targets the obliques and lateral core stabilizers, often recommended for people whose discomfort shows up more on one side during twisting or side-bending.
steps: Lie on your side, propped on your forearm, elbow under your shoulder.
Lift your hips so your body forms a straight line from head to feet.
Hold 10-20 seconds, keeping hips lifted and level.
Switch sides.
cautions: Drop to your knees for an easier version if a full side plank strains your shoulder.

name: Figure-Four Stretch
description: One of the most effective stretches for the piriformis and outer hip - frequently used for sciatica-adjacent tightness and general hip stiffness.
steps: Lie on your back, knees bent, feet flat.
Cross your right ankle over your left thigh, forming a '4' shape.
Reach through and pull your left thigh toward your chest until you feel a stretch in the right hip/glute.
Hold 20-30 seconds, then switch sides.
cautions: If you feel shooting pain down the leg (not just a local stretch), stop and consider seeing a clinician - this can indicate nerve involvement.

name: Kneeling Hip Flexor Stretch
description: Targets tight hip flexors from prolonged sitting, a very common contributor to hip and low-back tightness.
steps: Kneel on one knee (pad it with a cushion), other foot forward, knee bent 90 degrees.
Tuck your pelvis slightly and shift your weight forward until you feel a stretch in the front of the back hip.
Keep your torso upright.
Hold 20-30 seconds, switch sides.
cautions: Keep the front knee tracking over the ankle, not past the toes.

name: 90/90 Hip Stretch
description: A comprehensive hip mobility drill that addresses both internal and external rotation, often used by people who sit cross-legged or squat frequently.
steps: Sit with your front leg bent 90 degrees in front of you, back leg bent 90 degrees out to the side.
Keeping your chest tall, lean gently forward over the front leg.
Hold 20-30 seconds, then switch which leg is in front.
Repeat 2-3 times per side.
cautions: Go slowly if you have any knee sensitivity - keep pressure on the hip, not twisting through the knee.

name: Clamshell
description: Strengthens the hip stabilizers, commonly recommended for hip and even knee discomfort linked to weak glute medius muscles.
steps: Lie on your side, knees bent about 45 degrees, feet stacked and together.
Keeping feet touching, lift your top knee like opening a clamshell.
Lower with control.
Do 12-15 reps per side.
cautions: Keep your hips stacked - avoid rolling your pelvis backward to fake more range.

name: Standing Hip Abduction
description: A standing strengthening drill for the outer hip, useful for people whose hip or knee discomfort relates to weak hip stabilizers during walking.
steps: Stand holding a wall or chair for balance.
Keeping your leg straight and toes forward, lift it out to the side.
Lower with control without leaning your torso to compensate.
Do 12-15 reps per side.
cautions: Keep your torso upright - swinging the leg using momentum reduces the benefit.

name: Glute Bridge
description: Strengthens the glutes and low back extensors together, a common recommendation for general low-back and hip resilience.
steps: Lie on your back, knees bent, feet flat hip-width apart.
Squeeze your glutes and lift your hips until your body forms a straight line from shoulders to knees.
Hold 2-3 seconds at the top.
Lower with control and repeat 12-15 times.
cautions: Avoid overarching your low back at the top - stop the lift at a straight line.

name: Pigeon Pose
description: A deeper hip-opening stretch for the glutes and outer hip, useful for runners or anyone with deep hip tightness.
steps: From hands and knees, bring your right knee forward behind your right wrist, shin at an angle.
Slide your left leg straight back behind you.
Square your hips forward and fold over your front leg as far as comfortable.
Hold 30 seconds, switch sides.
cautions: Support the front hip with a cushion if the stretch is too intense; avoid if it strains the front knee.

name: Butterfly Stretch
description: A classic inner-thigh stretch, useful for groin tightness from sitting cross-legged, cycling, or lateral sports movements.
steps: Sit tall with the soles of your feet together, knees falling out to the sides.
Hold your feet and gently press your knees toward the floor with your forearms, or just let gravity work.
Hold 20-30 seconds, keeping your back straight rather than rounding forward.
Relax and repeat 2-3 times.
cautions: Ease into it - forcing the knees down can strain the groin or inner knee.

name: Standing Side Lunge
description: A dynamic inner-thigh stretch that also builds a bit of strength through the standing leg, good for groin tightness from lateral movement sports.
steps: Stand with feet wide apart, toes forward.
Shift your weight to one side, bending that knee while keeping the other leg straight.
Feel the stretch along the inner thigh of the straight leg.
Hold 2-3 seconds, then shift to the other side. Repeat 8-10 times per side.
cautions: Keep the bent knee tracking over the ankle, not caving inward.

name: Side-Lying IT Band Stretch
description: Addresses tightness along the outer thigh (iliotibial band), which can contribute to outer knee and hip discomfort, especially in runners.
steps: Lie on your side with the leg to be stretched on top, straight.
Let the top leg drop slightly behind you, off the edge of a bed or ledge if available, until you feel a stretch along the outer thigh.
Hold 20-30 seconds.
Switch sides.
cautions: The IT band itself stretches minimally - focus on a mild pull rather than forcing intensity.

name: Foam Rolling the IT Band
description: A self-myofascial release technique frequently used to ease outer-thigh tightness and tenderness.
steps: Lie on your side with a foam roller under your outer thigh, supporting yourself with your forearm and top leg.
Roll slowly from just below the hip to just above the knee.
Pause on any tender spots for 20-30 seconds.
Repeat for 1-2 minutes per side.
cautions: Use light-to-moderate pressure; avoid rolling directly over the knee joint itself.

name: Standing Hamstring Stretch
description: A simple, accessible stretch for tight hamstrings, which often contribute to both low-back and knee discomfort.
steps: Place one heel on a low step or curb, leg straight, toes pointing up.
Keeping your back straight, hinge forward from the hips until you feel a stretch in the back of the thigh.
Hold 20-30 seconds.
Switch legs.
cautions: Keep a slight bend in the standing knee for balance; don't round through the low back to reach farther.

name: Seated Slider (Hamstring Nerve Glide)
description: A gentler alternative to static stretching for hamstring tightness that also has a nerve-tension component, sometimes used when standard stretches feel irritating rather than relieving.
steps: Sit tall toward the front of a chair, one leg extended, heel on the floor.
Gently straighten the knee while flexing the ankle (toes up), then bend the knee again while pointing the toes.
Move slowly and rhythmically for 10-12 reps.
Switch legs.
cautions: This should feel like mild tension, not a stretch to the max - back off if it reproduces sharp or radiating pain.

name: Standing Quad Stretch
description: A classic stretch for the front of the thigh, useful for tightness after sitting or activities like cycling and running.
steps: Stand holding a wall or chair for balance.
Bend one knee, bringing your heel toward your glute, and hold your ankle or foot.
Keep your knees close together and hips level.
Hold 20-30 seconds, switch legs.
cautions: Avoid arching your low back to increase the stretch; pull the foot up rather than the thigh forward.

name: Couch Stretch
description: A deeper combined quad and hip flexor stretch popular for people who sit for long stretches of the day.
steps: Kneel in front of a couch or wall, back shin resting up against it, back foot pointing up.
Keep your front foot planted, torso upright, and gently squeeze the glute on the back leg.
Hold 20-30 seconds, working up to longer holds as it becomes comfortable.
Switch sides.
cautions: This is an intense stretch - ease into it gradually and pad your knee.

name: Terminal Knee Extension
description: A gentle strengthening drill for the muscles that stabilize the knee, often recommended for mild knee discomfort or after periods of reduced activity.
steps: Loop a resistance band around a sturdy anchor at knee height and around the back of your knee.
Step back until there's tension, standing with a very slight bend in the knee.
Straighten the knee fully against the band's resistance, squeezing the front of the thigh.
Do 2-3 sets of 12-15.
cautions: Avoid locking the knee harshly; the motion should be smooth and controlled.

name: Heel Slides
description: A gentle range-of-motion exercise for stiff knees, often used early in recovery from minor knee irritation or after long immobility.
steps: Lie on your back with legs straight.
Slowly slide one heel toward your glutes, bending the knee as far as comfortable.
Slide back out to straight.
Repeat 10-15 times per leg.
cautions: Move slowly within a pain-free range; sharp catching pain warrants medical follow-up.

name: Standing Toe Raises
description: Strengthens the muscle along the front of the shin, often recommended for shin tightness or mild shin-splint-type discomfort from walking or running.
steps: Stand with your heels on the floor, back against a wall for balance if needed.
Lift the balls of your feet and toes as high as comfortable, keeping heels down.
Lower with control.
Do 2-3 sets of 15-20.
cautions: Go slowly - this small muscle fatigues quickly and can cramp if rushed.

name: Kneeling Shin Stretch
description: Stretches the front of the shin and top of the foot, useful after activity that leaves the front of the lower leg feeling tight.
steps: Kneel on a soft surface with the tops of your feet flat on the floor, toes pointing back.
Sit back gently toward your heels until you feel a stretch along the shins and tops of the feet.
Hold 15-20 seconds.
Rise back up slowly.
targets: Tibialis anterior, extensor muscles of the foot
cautions: Go gently - this stretches sensitive structures on top of the foot and ankle.

name: Wall Calf Stretch
description: A go-to stretch for tight calves, which commonly contribute to ankle stiffness and heel discomfort.
steps: Stand facing a wall, hands on the wall for support.
Step one foot back, keeping it straight with the heel flat on the ground.
Lean into the wall until you feel a stretch in the back of the lower leg.
Hold 20-30 seconds, switch legs.
cautions: Keep the back heel firmly planted; don't let the back foot turn outward.

name: Bent-Knee Calf Stretch (Soleus)
description: Targets the deeper calf muscle that a straight-leg stretch misses, useful for ankle stiffness especially when squatting or going downstairs feels tight.
steps: Same setup as the wall calf stretch, but bend the back knee slightly while keeping the heel down.
Lean forward gently until you feel a stretch lower in the calf, near the Achilles.
Hold 20-30 seconds, switch legs.
cautions: Keep the heel on the ground throughout.

name: Standing Calf Raise
description: A simple strengthening move for the calves, useful for building resilience alongside calf and ankle stretches.
steps: Stand with feet hip-width apart, holding a wall or chair for balance if needed.
Rise up onto the balls of your feet as high as comfortable.
Lower with control.
Do 2-3 sets of 15-20.
cautions: Control the lowering phase rather than dropping quickly.

name: Ankle Circles
description: A simple, low-impact way to restore general ankle mobility, often used as a warm-up or after periods of immobility (like a cast or long travel).
steps: Sit or lie down and lift one foot off the ground.
Slowly rotate your ankle in a full circle, 10 times each direction.
Switch feet.
cautions: Keep the motion slow and pain-free.

name: Ankle Alphabet
description: A fun, thorough way to move the ankle through many directions, popular in early-stage rehab after ankle sprains or immobility.
steps: Sit with your leg extended, foot off the ground.
Using only your ankle and foot, 'write' the letters of the alphabet in the air.
Move slowly and with control.
Switch feet.
targets: Ankle joint mobility, lower leg muscles
cautions: Stop if any letter/motion causes sharp pain.

name: Kneeling Ankle Dorsiflexion Stretch
description: Improves the ankle's ability to bend the foot upward, a range of motion that's often limited and important for squatting, stairs, and walking uphill comfortably.
steps: Kneel in a half-kneeling position with the foot to stretch flat on the floor in front of you.
Keeping the heel down, gently drive your knee forward over your toes.
Hold 15-20 seconds at a mild stretch, or pulse gently 10-15 times.
Switch legs.
cautions: Keep the heel glued to the floor - if it lifts, you've gone too far.

name: Plantar Fascia Roll
description: A self-massage technique for the sole of the foot, commonly used for morning heel/arch discomfort associated with plantar fasciitis-type tightness.
steps: Sit and place a ball (tennis ball or similar) under the arch of your foot.
Roll it slowly from heel to toes, applying comfortable pressure.
Pause on tender spots for 20-30 seconds.
Continue for 1-2 minutes per foot.
cautions: Avoid if there is acute sharp heel pain - see a clinician; this is for general tightness/tenderness.

name: Toe Spreads
description: Builds strength and mobility in the small muscles of the foot, often neglected by supportive footwear.
steps: Sit with feet flat on the floor.
Spread your toes as wide apart as possible without curling them.
Hold 5 seconds, relax.
Repeat 10-15 times per foot.
cautions: None significant; go slowly if you have limited toe mobility.

name: Wrist Flexor Stretch
description: Relieves tightness on the palm side of the forearm/wrist, common with typing, lifting, or repetitive gripping.
steps: Extend one arm in front of you, palm up.
With your other hand, gently pull the fingers of the extended hand back and down toward the floor.
Hold 20-30 seconds, feeling the stretch along the inside of the forearm.
Switch sides.
cautions: Stretch gently - the wrist has many small structures that are easy to overstretch.

name: Wrist Extensor Stretch
description: Targets the top-of-forearm muscles associated with 'tennis elbow'-type discomfort and general wrist stiffness from typing or mousing.
steps: Extend one arm in front of you, palm facing down.
With your other hand, gently press the back of the hand downward and toward you.
Hold 20-30 seconds.
Switch sides.
cautions: A mild stretch is enough; avoid forcing if there's tenderness near the elbow.

name: Wrist Circles
description: A simple mobility warm-up for wrists that feel stiff after typing, lifting, or repetitive hand use.
steps: Clasp your hands together or make loose fists.
Slowly circle both wrists 10 times in each direction.
Shake out your hands afterward.
cautions: Keep the motion slow and pain-free.

name: Tendon Glide
description: A gentle finger and wrist mobility sequence often recommended for hand stiffness from repetitive typing or gripping.
steps: Start with fingers straight up like a 'stop' sign.
Bend fingers into a hook fist, then straighten.
Bend into a full fist, then straighten.
Bend into a straight fist, then straighten. Repeat the sequence 5-10 times.
cautions: Move slowly through each position; stop if any position causes sharp pain.

name: Eccentric Wrist Extension (Tennis Elbow)
description: A widely recommended exercise for lateral elbow discomfort ('tennis elbow'), focusing on slow lengthening of the forearm extensor muscles.
steps: Rest your forearm on a table, palm down, wrist hanging off the edge, holding a light weight (or a water bottle).
Use your other hand to lift the wrist into extension.
Slowly lower the weight over 3-5 seconds using only the working wrist.
Do 2-3 sets of 10-15 slow lowers.
cautions: Use very light resistance to start; sharp pain at the elbow means reduce load or stop and consult a clinician.

name: Golfer's Elbow Stretch
description: Addresses inner-elbow/forearm tightness ('golfer's elbow'), the counterpart to tennis elbow on the flexor side.
steps: Extend the affected arm in front of you, palm up, elbow straight.
With the other hand, gently pull the fingers and hand back into extension.
Hold 20-30 seconds, feeling the stretch along the inner forearm.
Repeat 2-3 times.
cautions: Keep it gentle - a sharp pinch near the elbow means back off.

name: Foam Roller Chest Opener
description: A passive stretch that opens the chest and front shoulders using a foam roller along the spine, complementing the doorway stretch.
steps: Lie lengthwise along a foam roller, supporting your head, hips level on the roller.
Let your arms fall open out to the sides, palms up.
Relax and breathe for 60-90 seconds, letting gravity open the chest.
cautions: Make sure the roller is stable; get on and off carefully.

name: Neck Flexion Stretch
description: Stretches the back of the neck, useful for tension that builds up from looking down at screens for long periods.
steps: Sit or stand tall.
Slowly lower your chin toward your chest until you feel a stretch along the back of the neck.
Optionally rest your hands on the back of your head for a light extra pull - no forcing.
Hold 20-30 seconds.
cautions: Keep any added hand pressure very light.

name: Levator Scapulae Stretch
description: Targets a common trigger-point spot at the base of the neck near the shoulder blade, often tender from stress or a poor sleeping position.
steps: Turn your head about 45 degrees to one side, then drop your chin toward your chest.
Gently rest the hand on that side on the back of your head for light overpressure.
Hold 20-30 seconds, feeling the stretch toward the shoulder blade.
Switch sides.
cautions: Use only light hand pressure - this spot is often sensitive.

name: Neck Extensor Stretch
description: Gently stretches the front of the neck, a less commonly addressed direction that can help balance out constant forward-head posture.
steps: Sit or stand tall.
Gently tip your head back and slightly lift your chin, looking toward the ceiling.
Hold only briefly at a very mild stretch, 5-10 seconds.
Return to neutral and repeat 3-5 times.
targets: Neck flexors, front of the throat
cautions: Keep this gentle and brief - avoid if it causes dizziness or neck discomfort.

name: Jaw Side-to-Side Glide
description: A mobility drill for lateral jaw movement, complementing straight-line jaw opening exercises.
steps: Relax your jaw with lips gently closed, teeth slightly apart.
Slowly slide your lower jaw to the right as far as comfortable.
Return to center, then slide left.
Repeat 8-10 times per side, moving slowly.
cautions: Stop if you feel clicking, catching, or pain rather than a mild stretch.

name: Resisted Jaw Opening
description: A gentle strengthening drill for the jaw-opening muscles, sometimes used alongside stretches for overall jaw stability.
steps: Place your thumb lightly under your chin.
Begin opening your mouth while pressing your thumb up gently to resist the motion.
Hold the effort for 5 seconds without letting your jaw fully open.
Relax and repeat 5-8 times.
cautions: Use very light resistance; this is not meant to be a hard push.

name: Shoulder Circles
description: A simple warm-up that moves the whole shoulder girdle through its range, good before activity or after long stretches of sitting.
steps: Stand tall, arms relaxed at your sides.
Roll your shoulders up, back, and down in a smooth circle.
Do 10 circles backward, then 10 forward.
cautions: Keep the motion smooth and unforced.

name: Sleeper Stretch
description: Targets internal rotation range at the shoulder, often recommended for overhead-throwing-type tightness or general shoulder stiffness.
steps: Lie on your side with the affected shoulder underneath, arm out in front at 90 degrees, elbow bent 90 degrees.
Using your other hand, gently press the forearm of the bottom arm down toward the floor.
Hold 20-30 seconds at a mild stretch.
Switch sides.
cautions: Press gently - this stretch is easy to overdo. Stop at mild tension, not pain.

name: Y-T-W Raises
description: A scapular-strengthening sequence that builds the muscles supporting good shoulder posture, popular as a posture-maintenance routine.
steps: Lie face down, or hinge forward at the hips while standing, arms hanging.
Raise your arms to form a 'Y' overhead, hold briefly, then lower.
Raise your arms out to a 'T' at shoulder height, hold, then lower.
Raise your arms out to a 'W' with bent elbows, hold, then lower. Repeat the sequence 8-10 times.
cautions: Use little to no weight at first - this is about control, not load.

name: Standing Chest Stretch
description: A no-equipment chest opener you can do anywhere, useful as a quick counter to hours of rounded-shoulder sitting.
steps: Stand tall and clasp your hands behind your back.
Straighten your arms and gently lift your hands away from your body.
Squeeze your shoulder blades together and lift your chest.
Hold 20-30 seconds.
cautions: Keep your neck relaxed - avoid jutting your chin forward.

name: Corner Stretch
description: A two-armed variation on the doorway stretch that opens both sides of the chest at once.
steps: Stand facing a corner, forearms on each wall, elbows roughly shoulder height.
Lean your body into the corner until you feel a stretch across the chest.
Hold 20-30 seconds.
Adjust arm height and repeat for a slightly different angle.
cautions: Lean in gradually; stop well short of shoulder pain.

name: Doorway Lat Stretch
description: Opens up the lats and side of the upper back, useful for tightness that limits reaching fully overhead.
steps: Hold a doorframe or sturdy post at about head height with one hand.
Walk your hips away and down slightly, letting your side body stretch.
Hold 20-30 seconds, feeling the stretch along your side and armpit.
Switch sides.
cautions: Keep a secure grip and don't let your feet slip.

name: Thoracic Extension Over Chair
description: A no-equipment alternative to the foam roller thoracic extension, useful for opening up a rounded upper back.
steps: Sit toward the front of a sturdy chair with a low back.
Place your hands behind your head and gently arch your upper back over the top of the chair back.
Hold 10-15 seconds at a comfortable stretch, then return upright.
Repeat 5-8 times.
cautions: Make sure the chair is stable; keep the stretch gentle.

name: Gentle Bicycle Crunch
description: A controlled core movement that works the obliques and rectus abdominis together, often used to build general trunk strength.
steps: Lie on your back, hands lightly behind your head, knees bent over your hips.
Slowly extend one leg out while rotating to bring the opposite elbow toward the bent knee.
Switch sides in a slow, controlled pedaling motion.
Continue for 10-12 reps per side.
cautions: Move slowly and keep your low back flat against the floor - this isn't about speed.

name: Bridge with March
description: Adds a core-stability challenge to the standard glute bridge, useful for building the hip and trunk control that supports the low back.
steps: Lie on your back, knees bent, feet flat, and lift into a bridge position.
Holding the bridge, slowly lift one foot a few inches off the floor.
Place it back down and lift the other foot.
Alternate for 8-10 reps per side, keeping your hips level throughout.
cautions: Stop if your hips drop or rock - that means the range is too big for now.

name: Standing Oblique Reach
description: A standing side-bend that stretches and gently activates the obliques, a simple option when getting on the floor isn't convenient.
steps: Stand with feet hip-width apart, one arm raised overhead.
Lean your torso to the opposite side, reaching the raised arm over your head.
Hold 15-20 seconds, feeling a stretch along your side.
Switch sides.
cautions: Keep the bend smooth and controlled, not a bounce.

name: Sphinx Pose
description: A gentle prone extension that can help ease a low back that's stiff from sitting, without the deeper effort of a full backbend.
steps: Lie face down, propped up on your forearms, elbows under your shoulders.
Let your low back relax and gently arch, chest lifted.
Hold 20-30 seconds, breathing steadily.
Lower back down to rest.
cautions: Keep it gentle - if it increases leg symptoms, stop and consider a medical evaluation.

name: Supine Spinal Twist
description: A relaxing rotational stretch for the low back and hips, often used to unwind tension at the end of the day.
steps: Lie on your back, knees bent, feet flat.
Let both knees fall gently to one side while keeping your shoulders flat on the floor.
Hold 20-30 seconds, breathing into the stretch.
Bring knees back to center and switch sides.
cautions: Let your knees fall only as far as feels comfortable; keep both shoulders down.

name: Standing Back Extension
description: A quick standing stretch that reverses the forward-flexed posture of sitting, often used throughout the day as a low-effort reset.
steps: Stand tall with hands supporting your lower back.
Gently lean backward, looking slightly upward, until you feel a mild stretch.
Hold 5-10 seconds.
Return to standing and repeat 5-8 times.
cautions: Keep the lean small and controlled; stop if it causes sharp pain.

name: Cross-Arm Triceps Stretch
description: A variation on the overhead triceps stretch for people whose shoulders don't love the fully overhead position.
steps: Bring one arm across your body at chest height, elbow bent.
Use your other hand to gently press the elbow further across.
Hold 20-30 seconds, feeling the stretch along the back of the upper arm.
Switch sides.
cautions: Press gently - avoid forcing extra range at the shoulder.

name: Resisted Curl and Stretch Flow
description: Combines light strengthening with a stretch at the end range, useful for building resilience in the biceps alongside flexibility work.
steps: Hold a light resistance band or light weight, arm at your side.
Slowly curl up, then slowly lower all the way down and let the elbow fully straighten.
At the bottom, hold a light stretch for 2-3 seconds before the next rep.
Do 10-12 slow reps per arm.
cautions: Use light resistance and controlled tempo rather than momentum.

name: Forearm Foam Roll
description: A self-massage technique for tight forearms from typing, gripping, or repetitive hand use.
steps: Rest your forearm on a foam roller or your other thigh.
Roll slowly from elbow to wrist, on both the top and underside of the forearm.
Pause on tender spots for 20-30 seconds.
Repeat on the other arm.
cautions: Use light-to-moderate pressure; avoid rolling directly over the wrist or elbow joints.

name: Prayer Stretch
description: A simple two-handed stretch for both forearms and wrists at once, easy to do at a desk.
steps: Bring your palms together in front of your chest, fingers pointing up, as if praying.
Slowly lower your hands toward your waist while keeping palms pressed together.
Hold at the point where you feel a stretch along the forearms and wrists, 20-30 seconds.
cautions: Lower only as far as comfortable - don't force your palms apart.

name: Wrist Flexion/Extension with Light Weight
description: A basic strengthening exercise for the wrist in both directions, often recommended for general wrist resilience.
steps: Rest your forearm on a table, wrist hanging off the edge, holding a light weight.
Slowly curl the wrist up, then lower fully down.
Do 12-15 reps, then turn your palm down and repeat lifting the back of the hand.
Switch arms.
cautions: Start with a very light weight - the wrist fatigues quickly.

name: Finger Extension Stretch
description: Targets the small muscles that extend the fingers, a nice counter-stretch for hands that spend a lot of time gripping or typing.
steps: Hold one hand out, fingers relaxed.
Use your other hand to gently pull the fingers and thumb back toward you.
Hold 15-20 seconds.
Switch hands.
cautions: Keep the pull light - fingers have small, sensitive joints.

name: Elbow Flexion/Extension ROM
description: A basic range-of-motion drill for a stiff elbow, often used after periods of reduced use or minor irritation.
steps: Sit with your arm resting on a table, palm up.
Slowly bend your elbow as far as comfortable, then straighten fully.
Move slowly and smoothly for 10-15 reps.
Switch arms.
cautions: Move within a pain-free range; catching or sharp pain warrants a medical check.

name: Forearm Pronation/Supination Stretch
description: Mobilizes the rotational movement of the forearm (turning your palm up and down), a range that's easy to neglect.
steps: Sit with your elbow bent 90 degrees and tucked at your side, holding a light object like a pencil.
Slowly rotate your forearm so your palm faces up, then down.
Move slowly through the full comfortable range for 10-12 reps.
Switch arms.
cautions: Keep your elbow tucked at your side so the motion comes from the forearm, not the shoulder.

name: Standing Hip Circles
description: A simple mobility warm-up that moves the hip through a wide range, good before activity or after long sitting.
steps: Stand holding a wall or chair for balance.
Lift one knee and draw a large circle with it, out to the side and around.
Do 8-10 circles, then reverse direction.
Switch legs.
cautions: Keep the circles smooth and within a comfortable range.

name: Seated Figure-4 Stretch
description: A desk-friendly version of the figure-four stretch for hip and glute tightness, no floor space required.
steps: Sit tall in a chair and cross one ankle over the opposite knee.
Keeping your back straight, hinge forward slightly from the hips.
Hold 20-30 seconds, feeling a stretch in the outer hip.
Switch sides.
cautions: Fold forward only as far as feels comfortable in the hip.

name: Standing Hip Flexor Wall Stretch
description: A standing alternative to the kneeling hip flexor stretch, useful when kneeling on the floor isn't comfortable.
steps: Stand an arm's length from a wall, facing away, and place the top of one foot on a low chair or step behind you.
Tuck your pelvis slightly and shift your hips forward until you feel a stretch in the front of that hip.
Hold 20-30 seconds.
Switch sides.
cautions: Use a stable support and keep your torso upright.

name: Fire Hydrant
description: A hip-strengthening exercise that targets the outer glutes, commonly paired with clamshells for hip stability work.
steps: Start on hands and knees.
Keeping your knee bent, lift one leg out to the side, like a dog at a fire hydrant.
Lower with control.
Do 12-15 reps per side.
cautions: Keep your hips level - avoid rotating your torso to lift the leg higher.

name: Single-Leg Glute Bridge
description: A more challenging version of the glute bridge that adds a single-leg stability component.
steps: Lie on your back, knees bent, feet flat.
Extend one leg straight out, then lift your hips using the other leg.
Hold 2-3 seconds at the top, keeping hips level.
Lower with control and repeat 8-10 times per side.
cautions: If your hips tilt or drop, go back to the two-leg bridge until you build more control.

name: Seated Piriformis Stretch
description: A gentle, chair-based way to reach the deep piriformis muscle, useful for outer-hip and glute tightness.
steps: Sit tall and cross one ankle over the opposite knee.
Place a hand on the crossed knee and gently press it down and away.
Hold 20-30 seconds.
Switch sides.
cautions: If you feel pain radiating down the leg rather than a local stretch, stop and consider a medical evaluation.

name: Piriformis Foam Roll
description: A self-massage technique that reaches the deep glute area, often used for tightness associated with sitting on a wallet or long periods of sitting.
steps: Sit on a foam roller or firm ball, crossing one ankle over the opposite knee.
Lean slightly toward the crossed side and roll slowly over the glute.
Pause on tender spots for 20-30 seconds.
Switch sides.
cautions: Use body weight to control pressure - ease off if it's too intense.

name: Frog Stretch
description: A deeper inner-thigh stretch than the butterfly, popular with athletes who need a lot of groin flexibility.
steps: Start on hands and knees, then widen your knees out to the sides as far as comfortable.
Keep your ankles in line with your knees, feet turned outward.
Rock your hips gently back toward your heels until you feel a stretch in the inner thighs.
Hold 20-30 seconds.
cautions: Ease into this gradually - it's an intense stretch for many people.

name: Standing Adductor Wall Stretch
description: A standing inner-thigh stretch using a wall for support, a simpler alternative to the floor-based butterfly or frog stretches.
steps: Stand side-on to a wall, one hand on the wall for balance.
Step the outside leg out to the side and bend that knee, keeping the near leg straight.
Shift your weight toward the bent knee until you feel a stretch in the straight leg's inner thigh.
Hold 20-30 seconds, switch sides.
cautions: Keep the bent knee tracking over the ankle, not caving inward.

name: Prone Quad Stretch
description: A lying-down alternative to the standing quad stretch, useful for people who find balancing on one leg uncomfortable.
steps: Lie face down on a mat.
Bend one knee and reach back to hold your ankle or foot.
Gently pull your heel toward your glute until you feel a stretch in the front of the thigh.
Hold 20-30 seconds, switch legs.
cautions: Keep your hips pressed into the mat rather than lifting to increase the stretch.

name: Wall Quad Stretch
description: A supported version of the standing quad stretch for anyone who wants extra balance assistance.
steps: Stand facing away from a wall, close enough to touch it, one hand on the wall for balance.
Bend one knee and hold your foot behind you with your free hand.
Keep your knees close together and hold 20-30 seconds.
Switch legs.
cautions: Avoid arching your low back to deepen the stretch.

name: Lying Hamstring Stretch (Towel-Assisted)
description: A supported hamstring stretch that lets you control the intensity precisely, often used in early-stage rehab settings.
steps: Lie on your back and loop a towel or strap around the ball of one foot.
Keeping that knee straight, use the towel to gently draw your leg toward you.
Hold at your first point of tension, 20-30 seconds.
Switch legs.
cautions: Keep your lower back flat on the floor rather than curling up to increase range.

name: Single-Leg Deadlift
description: A balance-and-strength movement that builds hamstring and glute control through a hip-hinge pattern, useful once basic hamstring flexibility feels comfortable.
steps: Stand on one leg, holding a wall or chair for balance if needed.
Hinge forward at the hips, extending the opposite leg back for balance, keeping your back flat.
Lower until you feel a stretch in the standing leg's hamstring, then return to standing.
Do 8-10 reps per side.
cautions: Move slowly and use support until your balance feels solid.

name: Standing IT Band Cross-Stretch
description: A standing option for outer-thigh tightness when lying down isn't convenient.
steps: Stand and cross one leg behind the other.
Lean your torso away from the back leg until you feel a stretch along its outer thigh.
Hold 20-30 seconds.
Switch sides.
cautions: Keep the lean controlled and hold onto something stable if needed.

name: Seated Knee Extension
description: A gentle range-of-motion and light strengthening drill for the knee, often used early in rehab or for general knee stiffness.
steps: Sit in a chair with your feet flat.
Slowly straighten one knee, lifting your foot until your leg is extended.
Hold 2-3 seconds, then lower with control.
Do 12-15 reps per leg.
cautions: Move smoothly - avoid kicking the leg up quickly.

name: Wall Sit
description: A static strengthening hold for the muscles around the knee, commonly used to build general knee resilience.
steps: Stand with your back against a wall and slide down until your knees are bent at a comfortable angle.
Hold the position, keeping your knees over your ankles.
Hold 15-30 seconds, building up gradually over time.
Rest and repeat 2-3 times.
cautions: Don't let your knees cave inward or go past your toes; stop if you feel joint pain rather than muscle fatigue.

name: Seated Ankle Dorsiflexion with Band
description: A light strengthening exercise for the muscle along the front of the shin, complementing standing toe raises.
steps: Sit with your leg extended and loop a resistance band around your foot, anchoring the other end.
Pull your toes and foot up toward your shin against the band's resistance.
Slowly return to start.
Do 2-3 sets of 15.
cautions: Use light resistance - this muscle is small and fatigues quickly.

name: Toe Taps
description: A simple bodyweight drill for shin endurance, useful as a warm-up or general lower-leg conditioning move.
steps: Stand with your heels on the ground, holding a wall for balance if needed.
Tap your toes up and down quickly and repeatedly, keeping heels planted.
Continue for 20-30 seconds.
Rest and repeat 2-3 times.
cautions: Stop if you feel cramping - this muscle can fatigue fast for beginners.

name: Downward Dog Calf Pump
description: A dynamic calf stretch that alternates between legs, commonly used as part of a warm-up flow.
steps: From hands and knees, tuck your toes and lift your hips up and back into an inverted V shape.
Bend one knee while pressing the other heel toward the floor, feeling a stretch in that calf.
Alternate slowly between legs, 'pumping' 8-10 times per side.
cautions: Bend your knees as much as needed to keep your back flat.

name: Seated Calf Stretch (Towel-Assisted)
description: A supported calf stretch you can do seated on the floor, useful when standing balance stretches aren't ideal.
steps: Sit with your leg extended and loop a towel around the ball of your foot.
Keeping your knee straight, gently pull the towel to draw your toes toward you.
Hold 20-30 seconds.
Switch legs.
cautions: Pull gently and stop at a mild stretch.

name: Resistance Band Ankle Eversion/Inversion
description: Strengthens the muscles on the inside and outside of the ankle, often recommended for general ankle stability, especially after a prior sprain.
steps: Sit with a resistance band looped around the outside of your foot, anchored to something stable.
Turn your foot outward against the band, then slowly return.
Switch the band to the inside of your foot and turn your foot inward against it.
Do 12-15 reps in each direction, each foot.
cautions: Use light resistance and controlled movement - avoid twisting through the knee.

name: Single-Leg Balance
description: A proprioception drill that builds the small stabilizing reflexes in the ankle and foot, commonly used after an ankle sprain or for general stability.
steps: Stand near a wall or counter for safety.
Lift one foot off the ground and balance on the other for 20-30 seconds.
Switch feet.
For more challenge, try it with your eyes closed (with support nearby).
cautions: Keep support within reach, especially if balance is a concern.

name: Towel Scrunches
description: Strengthens the small muscles along the bottom of the foot, often recommended alongside plantar fascia stretches.
steps: Sit with a small towel flat on the floor under one foot.
Using only your toes, scrunch the towel toward you.
Reset and repeat 10-15 times.
Switch feet.
cautions: None significant; go slowly if your toes cramp at first.

name: Short Foot Doming
description: A subtle but effective drill for building the arch-supporting muscles of the foot, often used for general foot resilience.
steps: Stand or sit with your foot flat on the floor.
Without curling your toes, try to draw the ball of your foot toward your heel, creating a slight dome in your arch.
Hold 5 seconds, then relax.
Repeat 10 times per foot.
cautions: This is a subtle movement - if your toes are curling, you're using the wrong muscles.
